You may not care for the sites, but I'd look in the alternative health media.
In order to be biologically available most elements need to be in an ionic or oxidized form. Potassium only has one state available to it, K+. So potassium in foods is all in the same state.
Oh I see. Sorry, not a chemist. I just see lots of potassium compounds as supplements (citrate, gluconate, ororate, etc.) and I was wondering if any of these compounds naturally occur in foods.

The molecules you named are simply anions. They can be used as a counter ion to potassium, a cation, to make a neutral compound. In order to make somethig a powder it needs to be neutral. Ions don't really care (solubility rules apply) what their counter ion is. When they hit water they go their separate ways. Table salt is a perfect example of an ionic substance. If you're interested in learning about this stuff take some of the beginning Chemistry series on Khan Academy.

A substance like potassium citrate is an ionic crystal. The potassium has a positive electric charge, and the citrate has a negative electric charge. When dry, they attract each other and line up into an orderly crystal. When dissolved in water, the potassium atoms and citrate molecules float away from each other.

In living things there are numerous negatively charged molecules. Chloride is by far the most common. Bicarbonate is also common. There are many others depending on which living thing you are talking about. Citrate is common in citrus fruit, which is how it gets its name.

All of the ones you named occur naturally. Your own body makes and uses vast amounts of citrate. It is a food that is entirely digested to produce carbon dioxide and energy, and makes urine more alkaline. Gluconate occurs naturally in the human body but it's mostly a waste product. It produces bulky supplement pills and does not affect urine alkalinity much. Orotate is digestible, and IIRC it is used because of a fad belief decades ago that it has special powers.

In potassium supplements they are probably allot the same. Chloride and citrate are smaller, good if you want to carry pills with you.
